# Alternating marker and separator-color gap fill

## When to Use
Use when a uniform-background grid contains sparse horizontal runs of equally spaced marker cells and the intended completion may alternate a second color into their gaps. Confirm with the current instance's demonstrations before applying this recurrence.

## Procedure
1. Record every marker coordinate and the background color.
2. Group aligned marker cells into observed horizontal runs; do not assume vertical runs are handled the same way without evidence.
3. For each run, add color 2 only to cells strictly between consecutive marker-7 cells, provided the demo establishes that color mapping.
4. Preserve markers, outside cells, and dimensions; mechanically validate row count and widths before submission.


## Confirmed recurrence: `task-3d904491` (one accepted instance)

The input is a uniform background (test color 5) with several isolated horizontal runs of marker 7. In a demo with background 9, each such run was completed as a fully alternating sequence: preserve the original 7 cells and place color 2 into every gap between consecutive 7s. This is local gap filling, not coloring an entire line or extending the pattern beyond the two outermost markers.

### Demo evidence (28×27)

- Row 0: 7 at columns 18 and 20; output inserted 2 at column 19.
- Row 7: 7 at columns 5, 7, 9; output inserted 2 at 6 and 8.
- Row 11: 7 at columns 5 and 7; output inserted 2 at 6.
- Row 16: 7 at columns 15, 17, 19, 21, 23; output inserted 2 at 16, 18, 20, 22.
- Row 24: 7 at columns 1 and 3; output inserted 2 at 2.
- All other cells unchanged. Background 9 varied from test background 5, while inserted color remained 2.

### Accepted test evidence (18×27)

Background 5. Runs were:
- Row 5: 7 at columns 3 and 5 → inserted 2 at column 4.
- Row 15: 7 at columns 9, 11, 13, 15, 17, 19, 21 → inserted 2 at columns 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20.
- Row 17: 7 at columns 14, 16, 18 → inserted 2 at columns 15 and 17.

The full output preserving all other cells was accepted.

### Additional accepted fresh recurrence: task-3d904491, 14×6 test with 14×17 demo

A new fresh instance was solved with one demonstration and zero wrong submissions. The demo used background 0, marker color 4, and inserted color 2. Across rows, the 4-markers appeared in horizontal runs; every strict interior cell between consecutive 4s on the same row was changed to 2, while marker cells and all cells outside the runs were unchanged. The demo included pairs and longer runs (including row 8 markers at columns 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, whose four interior cells became 2); it did not fill beyond outermost markers. This directly supported applying the horizontal-gap rule to the test despite a different marker/background palette.

Accepted test was 14×6, background 3, marker color 7. On rows 6 and 10 (zero-based), markers were at columns 1 and 3; each strict interior cell at column 2 changed to 2. Every other cell stayed 3 or remained its original marker, and the output retained all 14×6 dimensions. This is further direct evidence that the inserted color stays 2 while background and marker colors can vary. It reinforces only the row-wise horizontal operation; do not infer vertical filling.

### Additional confirmed recurrence: `task-3d904491` fresh 27×15 test with one demo (accepted after a malformed first submission)

Demo input was 13×21 with background 8 and marker 0. On each row, only background-colored cells strictly between consecutive 0 markers were changed to 2; the 0s and all exterior cells were preserved. The accepted test was 27×15, background 9, marker 8. For each row, fill every strict interior cell between consecutive 8s with 2, retaining all 8 markers and leaving all cells outside those intervals unchanged. Rows with no pair remain unchanged. The input's runs include pairs and longer runs; examples include row 0 markers at columns 1,3 (fill column 2), row 6 markers 5,7,9,11 (fill 6,8,10), and row 21 markers 4,6,8,10,12 (fill 5,7,9,11). This output was confirmed correct. The first submission on this instance was rejected as an invalid ARC grid because of a row-width/serialization error, not because of the transformation; generate from the parsed input and assert exactly 27 rows of 15 cells before returning JSON. This corroborates palette invariance (markers/background vary, inserted color stays 2) and strictly horizontal, bounded gap filling.

### Limits / caveat

This is one task-id recurrence evidence instance, not a universal ARC rule. One demo showed only horizontal runs, so vertical handling and the rationale for selecting rows/lines remain untested. In the observed test all runs were horizontal and clearly sparse; transform only gaps strictly between consecutive 7 markers, preserve marker 7 and all cells outside those gaps. Output must preserve input dimensions. This accepted test required an initial submission retry only because the first JSON accidentally had row-width errors; the corrected mechanically validated 18×27 grid was accepted. Generate arrays from an input copy and assert every row width before serializing to prevent that avoidable failure.

### Additional accepted recurrence: `task-3d904491` fresh 23×14 input (no demos)

A second fresh instance with the same task ID was accepted on the first submission without requesting demos. Background was color 8, marker cells were color 3, and the output inserted color 2 into every strict horizontal gap between consecutive 3s on each row. It preserved the 3 markers, all cells outside these gaps, and the 23×14 dimensions. The input contained scattered horizontal runs, including pairs and longer runs (e.g. the row with markers at columns 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 became an alternating 3/2 sequence across that interval); no cells were extended beyond the outermost markers. This is additional direct acceptance evidence for the same gap-fill recurrence across changed background and grid dimensions, still only establishing horizontal handling. The solver can apply the transformation deterministically: for each row, find all columns containing 3 and set cells strictly between each consecutive pair to 2; leave everything else untouched. Validate the exact row count and width before emitting the JSON action.

### Additional confirmed recurrence: `task-3d904491` fresh 11×20 test (one demo, one rejected output, then accepted)

This recurrence uses the same local horizontal-gap operation with palettes that differ from the previously accepted instances. Demo input used marker color 5 and gap/background color 4; output preserved every 5 and recolored only 4-cells strictly between consecutive 5s on each row to color 2. Examples include row 0's `5 4 5 4 5 4 5` becoming `5 2 5 2 5 2 5`; in row 2 the gap at column 7 remained 4 because it was not followed by another 5. Thus do not extend beyond the outermost marker or recolor every background/gap-colored cell.

For the fresh 11×20 test, the analogous marker color was 0, separator/background color 1, and inserted color remained 2. Recolor each 1 strictly between consecutive 0 markers on a row; preserve 0s and all other cells. The accepted output filled the omitted interior at row index 2, column 4 (between 0s at columns 3 and 5), as well as all other qualifying gaps. The first submitted output was rejected because it left this one obvious qualifying gap unchanged; the second, with all such horizontal gaps filled, was accepted. This is direct evidence for marker/separator palette variation within this task ID and confirms the row-wise rule; it does not establish vertical gap filling. Before submission, enumerate every row's marker positions and verify every consecutive-marker interior is recolored, with no changes outside those interiors.

"content": "---\nname: arc-demo-budget-strategy\ndescription: Use when choosing whether to request ARC demos.\nmetadata:\n  hermes:\n    tags: [arc, demonstrations, information-gain]\n    related_skills: [arc-grid-reasoning, arc-demo-hypothesis-audit]\n---\n\n# ARC demo-budget strategy\n\nUse when an ARC task charges for additional demonstrations or has a limited demo budget, particularly when the transformation's selector is unclear. The goal is not to exhaust the available examples; it is to gain enough discriminating evidence for a good decision while controlling request cost.\n\n## Procedure\n\n1. **Parse each pair into evidence.** Record exact changed cells and components, old/new colors, geometry, location, and unchanged alternatives. For object tasks use 4-connected components by default; test 8-connectivity only when diagonal contact could affect the rule.\n2. **Maintain a small explicit hypothesis set.** Phrase candidates as testable selectors and transformations, e.g. “largest non-background component,” “the unique shape matching an exemplar,” or “the component touching the guide line.” Avoid vague accounts like “the interesting object changes.”\n3. **Audit positive and negative examples.** Each hypothesis must predict the selected object in every demo and must not predict edits to observed unchanged objects. Keep object selection and replacement-color mapping as separate questions.\n4. **Plan before requesting.** Name the leading competing hypotheses and what feature of the next pair would distinguish them. If you cannot say how a possible result changes the ranking or action, the request has low information value.\n5. **Track information gain and diminishing returns.** After each demo, note whether hypotheses were eliminated or merely accumulated another compatible case. Do not request again just because a cap remains. If several varied demos fail to isolate a common property, recognize that evidence may be saturated or underdetermined.\n6. **Choose request vs submit by expected cost.** Request only when the next example could plausibly distinguish materially different rules and its expected value justifies its score cost versus a likely-wrong submission. If no useful request remains, make the best-supported deliberate choice rather than spending by default.\n7. **Preserve uncertainty.** Reaching the demo cap does not validate a guess. If the selector remains ambiguous, do not claim a visually plausible candidate is established; alter only cells warranted by the strongest supported hypothesis.\n8. **Honor the task interface.** When the environment requires exactly one JSON action, return exactly one action and no surrounding explanation.\n\n## Evidence ledger for changed-component tasks\n\n| Pair | Changed component | Before → after | Area / geometry | Position | Unchanged candidates |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n\nInclude unchanged same-color components and similar shapes. This guards against largest/smallest-object and color-only fallacies. `arc-demo-hypothesis-audit` has broader component auditing guidance; this skill focuses on deciding when an additional example is worth its cost.\n\n## Continual-ARC lesson: task-fba999ff\n\nThree requested demonstrations sufficed to identify the transform: connect same-color cells sharing a row or column by recoloring only strict interior cells to 3; endpoints and other cells remain unchanged. Demo palettes/backgrounds varied, while connector color stayed 3. In the fresh 5x25 test, only the two 8-markers at row 1, columns 12 and 14 had a gap, so one cell changed. Adjacent aligned marker pairs create no interior. This example rewarded careful sparse test audit; no fourth demo was needed after pair 3 showed extensive row/column segment completion and the test's sole gap was unambiguous.\n\n## Continual-ARC note: task-b335a605 tiny horizontal-band case\n\nOne test's unchanged-grid guess was wrong: the 4×4 input had full rows `[0,0,0,0]`, `[4,4,4,4]`, `[4,4,4,4]`, `[6,6,6,6]`. One demo showed a 7×7 analog where only the leading all-zero row changed, becoming the color of the bottom row (4); all other full-width bands, including duplicate adjacent colors, stayed exactly as input. The accepted test changed its top row to 6 (bottom-row color) and preserved all other rows. This is one branch-specific example, not a universal rule for task-b335a605: the task ID also recurs with periodic diagonal and horizontal patterns. A targeted demo was worth its cost because no-op and leading-row-from-bottom hypotheses predicted different outputs. See `puzzles:arc-grid-reasoning` reference `task-b335a605-tiny-horizontal-bands.md`.\n\n## Continual-ARC note: task-b335a605 horizontal stripe residues\n\nA separate accepted 28×28 instance with three nonzero full-width stripes (row 0 color 5, row 4 color 3, row 20 color 7) used stripe count `k=3` as the vertical period: each stripe's color fills its row residue modulo 3, yielding repeated `[5,3,7]`. Three demos supported this rule with different stripe counts/palettes; crucially, line colors are keyed by row modulo stripe count, not by numeric ordering. This is a separate recurrence branch from the tiny leading-row case and from diagonal periodic variants. See `puzzles:arc-grid-reasoning` reference `task-b335a605-horizontal-row-residue-pattern.md`.\n\n## Accepted recurrence note: task-2e5d2205 paired vertical edge runs (25×6)\n\nA fresh test with no demos was accepted with zero wrong submissions, adding confirmation to the paired equal-length opposing-edge-run branch: background 6; color-3 vertical runs of length 4 at right edge rows 0–3 and left edge rows 19–22; color-7 markers in the left run at `(20,3),(21,4),(22,2)`. Markers became 4 and their rows filled with 7 inward toward the left edge (c1–2, c1–3, c1), preserving edge 3. Corresponding offsets in the opposite right-edge run filled rows 1–3 across c0–4, preserving right edge 3; row 0 and all unselected rows remained unchanged. See `arc-ray-projection/references/task-2e5d2205-edge-run-correspondence-25x6-accepted.md` for the exact accepted grid. This reinforces the paired equal-length-run rule only; do not apply it to geometrically different unresolved recurrences with the same ID.\n\n## Unsolved recurrence note: task-7c19c728 with mixed diagonal pairs\n\nA 25×6 test was not solved after eight wrong submissions and two demos, despite two demos supporting diagonal same-color pair rays. Input (0-based) contained background 3; 4 at `(21,4),(22,3)`, 9 at `(22,2),(23,3)`, and 1 at `(23,2),(24,1)`. Demo 1 extended a 7-pair down-left and a 4-pair down-right; demo 2 extended a 6-pair down-left, painting through background until edge/blocker. Applying the apparent ray rule to the 9 and 4 pairs predicted 9 at `(20,0),(21,1),(24,4)` and 4 at `(20,5)`. This was rejected, including after removing the mistaken extra 4 at `(21,5)`; no candidate was accepted. The 1 pair appeared blocked on one side and boundary-limited on the other, but its exact relevance is unresolved. Treat this as uncertainty/negative evidence, not a validated transformation or selector. For future instances with multiple mixed-color/overlapping pairs, request a targeted demo before committing; do not overinterpret binary rejections.\n\n## Continual-ARC recurrence note: task-b335a605 periodic diagonal-stripe completion\n\nA solved fresh instance (19×19, zero wrong submissions) and four varied demos establish a diagonal-stripe periodic fill branch. Treat this separately from the task ID's horizontal stripe-residue and tiny horizontal-band branches: recurring IDs may present different transformations on fresh inputs.\n\n**Rule supported by these pairs:** Identify the parallel colored diagonals and their integer intercept/index. For down-right diagonals use `c-r`; for down-left diagonals use `r+c`. Find the smallest positive period `p` for which every observed diagonal index congruent modulo `p` has a consistent color. Fill every cell by the color assigned to its diagonal-index residue. Preserve the input dimensions. If a residue is represented by multiple observed lines, their colors must agree; do not impose an unobserved palette ordering.\n\n**Evidence ledger:**\n- Demo 1 (12×12): down-right diagonals; observed `c-r` indices 0→3, 4→4, 7→2, 8→6, 11→8. The output is periodic in `c-r` with period 6; residues 0…5 map `[3,2,6,6,4,8]`.\n- Demo 2 (29×29): only color-2 diagonals were marked; output is uniformly 2, consistent with the minimum period 1.\n- Demo 3 (22×22): down-left diagonals; `r+c` indices 1→5, 2→6, 7→8, 28→9. Output repeats with period 4, mapping residues 0…3 to `[9,5,6,8]`.\n- Demo 4 (28×28): down-right diagonals; `c-r` indices 14→3, −4→6, −21→6, −27→8. Output repeats with period 4, mapping residues 0…3 to `[6,8,3,6]`.\n- Accepted test (19×19): down-left diagonals with sums 3→1, 9→8, 19→9, 25→6, 27→4, 29→4, 35→2. Smallest consistent period is 7; residues 0…6 map `[2,4,8,1,6,9,4]`. Accepted output is `out[r][c] = map[(r+c) mod 7]`.\n\n**Practical caution:** infer orientation from the marked diagonals (slope), not from a favored formula. Use the smallest consistent modular period rather than guessing the grid width or number of colored cells. A single-color example cannot distinguish periods and only supports the constant-color special case; when multicolor input lines permit materially different periods, a targeted demo can be useful. This is direct task-ID recurrence evidence, not a universal ARC rule.\n\n## Common pitfalls\n\n- **Demo-cap completionism:** treating all available requests as a target rather than a limit.\n- **Unspecified information gain:** requesting “another example” without naming what uncertainty it could resolve.\n- **Positive-only reasoning:** tracking only the changed object, not unchanged lookalikes.\n- **Selector/mapping conflation:** guessing the output color while still unsure which object is selected.\n- **Binary-feedback overreach:** interpreting a rejected full-grid submission as identifying a particular wrong cell or assumption.\n- **False certainty after saturation:** mistaking a long list of varied examples for a discovered rule when no common discriminating property has been tested.\n\nFor the recurring component-recoloring case where eight demonstrations did not establish a selector, see `references/unresolved-component-recoloring.md`.", "path": separators, counting]\n    related_skills: [arc-grid-reasoning, arc-demo-action-discipline]\n---\n\n# Tiled exact-two marker count\n\n## Trigger\nA grid is divided by full separator rows and columns into repeated rectangular tiles, with each tile mostly a common background and containing sparse cells of a marker color. Outputs may be much smaller and have one cell per tile.\n\n## Procedure\n1. Identify and exclude complete separator rows/columns; count resulting tile rows and columns.\n2. For each tile independently, count marker-color cells (not connected components or occupied rows/columns).\n3. Test candidate predicates against every demo tile. In the recorded recurrence below, output `1` exactly when a tile contains exactly two marker cells; otherwise output the dominant tile color. Establish output background from evidence; do not copy it blindly.\n4. Build one output cell per tile. [\"arc-grid-reasoning\", \"arc-demo-hypothesis-audit\"], \"content\": \"---\\nname: arc-ray-projection\\ndescription: Use when ARC edge patterns project rays across a grid.\\nversion: 1.0.0\\nlicense: MIT\\nmetadata:\\n  hermes:\\n    tags: [arc, grid-puzzles, ray-projection, geometry]\\n    related_skills: [arc-grid-reasoning, arc-demo-hypothesis-audit]\\n---\\n\\n# ARC edge-ray projection\\n\\nUse this skill when repeated structures or colored cells on a grid boundary appear to define inward lines, bands, or rays, possibly interacting with interior markers. The source may lie on any edge; determine orientation from geometry rather than assuming horizontal or vertical propagation.\\n\\n## Evidence-first method\\n\\n1. **Parse the boundary source and interior objects.** Record exact coordinates, colors, contiguous runs, and whether apparent source cells form one component or several. Also record singleton/marker cells and background color.\\n2. **Calculate exact demo deltas.** Identify every painted ray cell, marker recolor, unchanged source cell, and unchanged lookalike. Distinguish source pixels from projected pixels; edge source patterns are often preserved.\\n3. **Infer geometry and emission rule separately.** Edge location determines the candidate inward normal. Demonstrations must establish which source rows/columns emit, whether a run emits as a unit or individual sources do, and how multiple edges interact.\\n4. **Infer interactions with markers.** A ray may stop at, pass through, or recolor a marker. Record whether a marker's color chooses the ray color and whether the marker is replaced (one demonstrated variant changes marker cells to 4). Do not assume color-4 replacement in a new task.\\n5. **Audit missing rays.** If similar edge sources yield different projections, treat omissions as important negative evidence. Check alignment, object segmentation, parity, paired sources, and marker relations against all demos; do not invent an unsupported universal rule.\\n6. **Project from the original grid.** Decide all rays before editing. Preserve source structures and unrelated cells unless a demo shows otherwise. Resolve overlaps only from evidence.\\n7. **Validate the complete result.** Compare predicted edits to each demo, then check dimensions, bounds, row widths, marker handling, source preservation, and untouched regions in the test.\\n\\n## Demo budgeting\\n\\nRequest another demonstration only when a concrete ambiguity could change the result—for example, whether a projection stops at the first marker, whether a contiguous boundary run emits every row, or whether the opposite edge also projects. State the distinguishing prediction mentally before requesting; a generic extra pair is not automatically useful.\\n\\n## Known evidence and caveat\\n\\nA Continual-ARC case established rays inward from edge stripes, preservation of source stripes, and interior marker conversion to 4; its test was accepted. One demo nevertheless had an apparently similar stripe row without an output ray, so the exact selector was not resolved. Treat this as evidence for the broad family, not proof of an unconditional per-edge-cell rule. The coordinate ledger and accepted test case are in `references/boundary-ray-projection.md`.\\n\\nA second solved case, `task-2e5d2205`, involved left/right edge stripes, color-7 marker cells and edge-row projections; its demos likewise contained omitted stripe rows. The accepted test output and full demo evidence are in `references/task-2e5d2205-notes.md`. Use as case-specific evidence only; notably, on the test the two-cell interior vertical marker was recolored to 4 and drew color 7 leftward from the left edge across its rows, while right-edge rows 0–1 projected 7 leftward and row 2 stayed unchanged.\\n\\n### Additional accepted recurrence: offset opposing edge runs (29×8)\\n\\nA fresh instance was accepted on its first submission after two demos. Equal-length runs occupied opposite edges at translated positions; interior markers within the span of one run became 4 and projected their original color toward that nearby edge source, while corresponding positions on the opposite run projected the same color across the interior. Demo 1 (12×8) used left/right color-1 runs at rows 0–4 and 6–10, with color-0 markers at `(7,5),(9,5)`: markers became 4, c6 on those rows became 0, and corresponding opposite rows 1 and 3 filled c1–7 with 0; other source rows were unchanged. Demo 2 (6×19) rotated this to top/bottom color-2 runs at row 0 c14–18 and row 5 c5–9; color-9 markers `(1,6),(2,5),(2,8),(2,9)` became 4, projected toward the bottom source, and counterpart top-run columns c14,c15,c17,c18 filled rows 1–5. In the accepted test, 29×8, top row c6–7 and bottom row c0–1 were color 9; markers 2 at `(3,0),(12,1)` became 4, columns c0 rows 4–27 and c1 rows 13–27 filled with 2 toward the bottom run, and counterpart columns c6–7 filled rows 1–28 with 2. Preserve edge sources and do not project from every unmarked edge location. Full delta ledger is in `references/task-2e5d2205-offset-paired-edge-runs-29x8.md`. This is a distinct recurrence branch and does not resolve task-2e5d2205's other unresolved variants.\\n\\n### Further accepted recurrence: task-2e5d2205, corresponding edge runs and inward marker rays (24×27)\\n\\nA second accepted recurrence confirms the same pattern on a 25×6 test with no demos: color-3 runs of length 4 occupied right-edge rows 0–3 and left-edge rows 19–22; color-7 markers on left-run rows 20–22 became 4, with 7 filling inward toward the left boundary, and opposite corresponding rows 1–3 were filled 7 across columns 0–4 while preserving the right-edge 3. Row 0 and unselected rows stayed unchanged. Full exact grid and spans are in `references/task-2e5d2205-edge-run-correspondence-25x6-accepted.md`.\\n\\nOne demo plus a fresh accepted test (zero wrong submissions) establish a case-specific operation for paired equal-length vertical edge runs. Interior markers within one edge run's row span become 4; fill the cells between each marker and its associated edge inward ray in the marker/edge direction, preserving the edge source. At corresponding within-run row offsets in the opposite edge run, fill the full interior width with color 7, preserving the opposite boundary. In the accepted 24×27 test, right edge 9 occupied rows 2–11, left edge 9 rows 14–23, and 7 markers at `(2,11),(3,23),(4,17),(6,23),(8,3),(11,15)` (zero-based) became 4. Their rightward 7 spans were respectively c12–25, c24–25, c18–25, c24–25, c4–25, and c16–25. Corresponding opposite-run rows `r+12 = 14,15,16,18,20,23` were filled 7 across c1–26, leaving left-edge c0=9. The 29×21 demo had left run rows 3–14, right run rows 17–28, 6 markers inside the left run; their rows projected leftward to c1, while opposite rows `r+14` were filled across c0–19, preserving right-edge c20=8. Exact evidence, coordinates, and changed-span lists are in `references/task-2e5d2205-edge-run-correspondence-accepted.md`. This is not a universal rule for every recurrence of this task ID; re-identify edge runs, lengths, sides, and marker rows. It does not resolve the separate unsolved 14×11 recurrence below.\\n\\n### Additional unresolved recurrence: task-2e5d2205 (14×11 test)\\n\\nA fresh occurrence with edge runs of 2 and three interior 3 cells remained unsolved after eight demos and eight rejected submissions. Its demonstrations consistently changed interior markers to 4 but showed varied, selectively omitted edge projections; no common selector was established. This is distinct from the older accepted and unresolved occurrences recorded elsewhere for the same task ID. Do not transplant prior task-ID rules. See `references/task-2e5d2205-current-unsolved-recurrence.md` for the complete eight-demo delta ledger, test coordinates, rejected hypothesis families, and validation cautions. No output from this occurrence should be treated as correct.\\n\\n## Common mistakes\\n\\n- Drawing a ray from every visible edge pixel despite contrary unchanged rows in demonstrations.\\n- Assuming all interior cells of a particular color are generic obstacles or markers without tracking exact deltas.\\n- Painting over the edge sources or unrelated background.\\n- Stopping at a marker when the demos show the ray passes through, or replacing a marker without evidence.\\n- Choosing ray color from convention instead of the demo mapping.\\n- Using a candidate rule that explains changed cells but ignores absent projections.\\n\\n## Recurrence: task-7c19c728 diagonal-pair continuation\\n\\nEight demos plus the accepted test establish that a same-color diagonal pair is extended outward along its diagonal through background cells to the grid edge or nearest occupied blocker. Keep the pair intact; do not overwrite any non-background cell. Test pair: color-6 cells (3,14),(4,13), background 9. The up-right continuation is blocked by color 3 at (2,15), while the down-left continuation paints (5,12) through (13,4), inclusive. See the full recurrence ledger in `puzzles/arc-grid-reasoning`.\\n\\nA major observed failure mode was coordinate drift when retyping the candidate array. Mechanically construct from the input and check dimensions (14x25 here), ray coordinates, preservation of all original non-background cells, and exact serialized output before submitting.\\n\\n### Accepted recurrence: task-7c19c728 diagonal-pair rays (26×27)\\n\\nA fresh 26×27 test was accepted first try after three demos. Multiple diagonal same-color pairs project outward along their diagonal through background cells only, stopping at the first occupied cell of any color or at the grid edge; preserve pair seeds, blockers, and unrelated cells. Horizontal/vertical extra contact does not itself define a ray, and isolated non-background singletons remain unchanged. The test's 9 pair at `(16,21),(17,22)` projected NW to `(0,5)`, while its SE ray was immediately blocked by 1 at `(18,23)`; color-1 vertical pair and color-5 singleton were preserved. Full demo/test coordinate ledger and caveats: `references/task-7c19c728-diagonal-pair-rays-26x27.md`.\\n\\n### Further accepted recurrence: task-7c19c728, four simultaneous diagonal pairs (13×23)\\n\\nFresh test accepted with zero demos beyond the first and zero wrong submissions. Background 2. Four diagonal same-color pairs each project outward from both ends along their own diagonal, through background 2 only; stop at any occupied cell or grid edge and preserve blockers. Input pairs (0-based): 8 at `(2,14),(3,15)` (down-right); 7 at `(2,17),(3,16)` (down-left); 5 at `(4,15),(5,14)` (down-left); 3 at `(4,16),(5,17)` (down-right). Accepted extensions: 8 at `(1,13),(0,12)`; its opposite ray is blocked by 3 at `(4,16)`. 7 at `(1,18),(0,19)`; its opposite ray is blocked by 5 at `(4,15)`. 5 at `(6,13),(7,12),(8,11),(9,10),(10,9),(11,8),(12,7)`; its opposite ray is blocked by 7 at `(3,16)`. 3 at `(6,18),(7,19),(8,20),(9,21),(10,22)`; its opposite ray is blocked by 8 at `(3,15)`. Output remained 13×23. This confirms multiple distinct colors/pair orientations can all project in the same grid, with each ray independently clipped by the first non-background blocker or boundary.\\n\\nThe one demo (14×16, background 7) contained four such pairs: 6 at `(7,8),(8,9)`, 4 at `(7,11),(8,10)`, 8 at `(9,9),(10,8)`, and 9 at `(9,10),(10,11)`. Their extensions were respectively: 6 NW to `(0,1)`; 4 NE from `(7,11)` through `(6,12),(5,13),(4,14),(3,15)`; 8 SW to `(13,5)`; and 9 SE to `(13,14)`. Rays in the opposite directions were blocked by existing pairs/cells: 6 by 9 at `(9,10)`, 4 by 8 at `(9,9)`, 8 by 4 at `(8,10)`, and 9 by 6 at `(8,9)`. The demo further supports that blockers are any occupied non-background color, not only a matching color. Use actual grid bounds; these projections terminate at the edge or at the first blocker.\\n\\nThis recurrence does not resolve the previously unsolved mixed-pair 25×6 case: preserve that separate selector uncertainty. Re-detect every same-color diagonal adjacent pair in a fresh input, project each outward ray from its endpoints, and mechanically validate exact dimensions and blockers before submitting.\\n\\n### Additional accepted recurrence: task-7c19c728, blocked pair/no-op test (7×24)\\n\\nA fresh test was accepted with one demo and no wrong submissions. The demo (9×23, background 1) contained a diagonal down-right pair of 5s at `(4,13),(5,14)` and a down-left pair of 7s at `(6,14),(7,13)`. Output extended the 5 line backward up-left from `(4,13)` to `(0,9)` and extended the 7 line forward down-left from `(7,13)` to `(8,12)`; all unrelated cells remained unchanged. This supports projecting pair lines outward through background to the boundary or first occupied blocker. In the accepted test, background was 2; 7s at `(0,5),(1,4)` formed a down-left diagonal pair. Its continuation from `(1,4)` toward `(2,3)` was blocked immediately by color 1, so no cells changed. Other isolated cells (6 at `(1,3)` and 1 at `(2,3)`) were preserved, as was the adjacent vertical 7 at `(2,4)`, which is not part of the diagonal pair. The correct output was exactly the input. This confirms that a pair can yield a no-op when blocked, and that isolated cells or non-diagonal contacts do not themselves project. Nous Research\\nmetadata:\\n  hermes:\\n    tags: [arc, grid-puzzles, translation, boundary]\\n    related_skills: [arc-grid-reasoning, arc-demo-hypothesis-audit]\\n---\\n\\n# Full-height boundary and block translation\\n\\nUse when an ARC grid has a full-height vertical marker line of a distinctive color and a separate patterned block with a horizontal gap between them. A demonstrated transformation moves the block toward the marker until the block's bounding box is adjacent to the marker, then traces the block's vacated far edge with another color.\\n\\n## Instance evidence: task-3af739a9\\n\\nDemo pair (13×9): marker color 2 occupies the full-height rightmost column (col 8). Patterned color-0 block's bounding box spans cols 2–4; the three-column gap is cols 5–7. In the output the block shifts right by three columns to cols 5–7, directly adjacent to marker col 8. A full-height color-8 line is added at the original far/left edge, col 2. The rest of the background and marker remain unchanged.\\n\\nAccepted fresh test (25×22): marker color 2 is full-height at col 6. Patterned color-4 block bounding box spans cols 8–14; the one-column gap is col 7. The accepted output shifts the pattern left one column, placing its bounding box at cols 7–13, adjacent to the marker. The full-height color-8 trace is at the original far/right edge, col 14. Pattern pixels retain color 4 and their exact internal holes. The marker line and unrelated background are unchanged.\\n\\nThe first attempted answer wrongly placed the trace at the near/marker-side edge (col 8), overwriting a translated motif cell. The accepted result confirms the trace belongs at the original far edge, away from the marker, not at the block's new boundary. The apparent shift magnitude is the blank gap between marker and block, not block width. Demos establish this exact rule strongly, but as usual contradictory future recurrence evidence should take precedence.\\n\\n## Procedure\\n\\n1. Find the full-height marker line and patterned block; determine the block's horizontal bounding box, including its blank cells/holes only insofar as needed to establish bounds.\\n2. Compute the number of blank columns between the marker and the block. Translate the entire pattern toward the marker by that many columns, making the block bbox adjacent to the marker.\\n3. Draw a full-height trace in color 8 immediately outside the translated block bbox on the side away from the marker: one column left of the translated bbox when moving right, one column right when moving left. This may coincide with the block's original far edge when there was a nonzero gap.\\n4. Preserve all motif pixels; the trace is outside the translated bbox and should not overwrite motif cells. Preserve all other cells.\\n5. Validate dimensions, row widths, exact translations and trace before output.\\n\\n## Additional recurrence evidence: task-3af739a9 accepted test (9×27)\\n\\nThe test had color-9 background, a full-height color-2 marker at column 16, and color-5 cells at `(4,15)` and `(5,14)` (0-based). The pattern bbox at columns 14–15 was already adjacent to the marker, so it did not translate. The accepted output preserves both 5s and adds a full-height color-8 trace at column 13, immediately outside the pattern bbox on the side away from the marker. The first rejected submission put the trace at column 14 and changed motif/background placement; this was rejected. The requested demo independently showed a shape shifted three columns toward a full-height color-2 guide and a full-height color-8 trace immediately beyond the shifted shape on its far side (demo columns: guide c4; original pattern bbox c8–15; translated bbox c5–12; trace c13). Thus trace position is relative to the post-translation bbox, not unconditionally a column within the original bbox. The accepted no-gap test confirms the trace is still one cell outside the far side when translation distance is zero.\\n\\n## Pitfalls\\n\\n- Do not shift by the block width; shift by the gap so the block ends adjacent to the marker.\\n- Do not paint the trace at the edge nearest the marker. Preserve all outline and exterior cells. This family belongs under topology/enclosure reasoning, not marker-anchored stencil copying.\\n\\n## Detecting stencil-shaped targets in noisy backgrounds\\n\\nSome tasks have no isolated marker cells: the target is every translated placement of the source motif's non-background cells that currently lie entirely on the uniform background. Search the full grid for embeddings of the exemplar's support mask (not merely runs or visually similar clusters), and recolor those matched cells with the motif color. The exemplar may be multi-cell and irregular; constrain all support offsets relative to one fixed anchor. Keep the exemplar intact. If placements overlap, write the motif color to the union of matched support cells. Search translations where every support offset lands on the marker color, then recolor those matched support cells to the source foreground color. # task-03bf78ba: unresolved 2-path through 8-barrier recurrence

## Trigger and status
Use when a fresh Continual-ARC task labelled `task-03bf78ba` shows a singleton 2 among zeros and repeated line-like patterns of 8s with gaps. This record is from one fully demonstrated but unsolved instance (three demos and eight rejected outputs). **There is no validated final rule or accepted test output.** Task IDs recur with fresh inputs; do not treat the layouts or rejected candidates below as an answer. Re-identify the geometry and use demos in a fresh instance if available.

## Direct observations from the three demos

All three demos preserve the 8 cells and original 2 seed and add color 2 to selected zero cells, retaining grid dimensions. Edits form thin, orthogonally connected path/branch-like lines through or near gaps in the 8 patterns. They are not ordinary connected-component flood fill: in the demonstrations, many zeros remain unchanged even though they are connected to the seed through the zero background. The selector/routing rule remains unresolved.

### Demo 1 (11×17)
Seed 2 at `(0,7)`. Horizontal 8 rows are r2, r4, r7, with gap columns respectively `{5,9}`, `{2,12}`, `{5}`. Output added 2 at exactly:
- r1, c5–9;
- r2, c5 and c9 (the existing 8 row's gaps);
- r3, c2–12;
- r4, c2 and c12;
- r5, c2 and c12;
- r6, c0–16 (the whole row);
- r7, c5 (the gap);
- r8–10, c5.
All other cells were preserved. This yields a connected, branched network of added 2s from the seed to the lower boundary, but the reason for the span/endpoints and full-width r6 is not established.

### Demo 2 (11×12)
Seed 2 at `(3,0)`. Vertical 8 columns include c2, c5, c9, with variable holes. Output added 2 at:
- c1, rows 0–5;
- row 3, c4 and c6–8;
- c4, rows 3–10;
- row 5, c2–4;
- row 6, c8–11.
All other cells were preserved. The 2 pattern again makes an orthogonal network of branches aligned with some 8-barrier gaps. Many available zeros remain untouched; simple flood fill and unconditional rays are unsupported.

### Demo 3 (10×13)
Seed 2 at `(4,12)`. Vertical 8 columns are c2, c5, c9, with gaps at differing rows. Output added 2 at:
- c6, rows 0–7;
- row 2, c7–10;
- row 3, c10;
- row 4, c10–12 (including the seed at c12, already 2);
- row 5, c6–10;
- row 8, c0–6.
All other cells were preserved. This confirms orientation/layout varies and does not support a fixed left-to-right or top-to-bottom projection rule.

## Rejected hypothesis families / cautions

- Flooding every zero reachable from the seed fails: demos leave extensive connected background unpainted.
- Filling all zeros or complete grid rows/columns fails; the added pixels are selective path-like segments.
- Filling corridors by guessed gap-to-gap spans (e.g. connecting every opening in adjacent 8 rows, or drawing every line adjacent to an 8 stripe) was not validated.
- In the single test instance paired with these demos, eight different submissions were rejected. They varied among flood fill, corridor/maze path guesses, full row/column spans, and adjustments to selected connections; therefore none of these candidate outputs is evidence of correctness. Do not reuse them.
- Binary rejection gives no cell-level diagnosis. Change only a hypothesis supported by exact demo deltas; avoid another arbitrary variant.

## Recommended handling on a future recurrence

1. Parse every 8 stripe and enumerate its exact zero gaps; mark seed coordinate.
2. For each new demo, compare exact changed-cell coordinates and preserve all unchanged zeros as negative evidence. Record path connectivity, orientation, endpoints, branches, boundary contacts, and whether lines stop at a blocker or turn at gaps.
3. Keep several explicit routing hypotheses and test each against every changed and unchanged cell. In particular distinguish all-gap connectivity, nearest-gap routing, rays from the seed, and a particular maze traversal; none is currently confirmed.
4. Spend a demo only if it can distinguish competing route rules. Because this recurrence's previous demos varied orientation and barrier placement but did not isolate a common routing selector, do not assume a generic completion after seeing only superficial similarity.
5. Construct the output from a copy of the current grid and validate exact dimensions, row widths, and unchanged barriers. Treat any proposed path rule as tentative until every demo is predicted exactly.
